title: Folding Carton Closures: Tuck End, Lock Bottom or Auto Bottom?
seoTitle: Folding Carton Closure Selection | MTT Packaging
summary: Compare folding carton closures by product weight, packing method and opening. Use a sample checklist to choose a workable structure before artwork approval.
intro: Choose a folding carton closure around the filled product, the packing method and the way the customer opens it. Tuck ends, manually locked bottoms and pre-glued auto bottoms solve different assembly problems. None has a universal load capacity. Compare physical samples using the same product and board specification, then approve the closure, insert and artwork together before production.
imageAlt: Skincare folding carton design reference with an auto-bottom structure
sections: Define how the carton will be packed

A bottle loaded from the top places different demands on the base from a light accessory loaded through either end. Record the filled weight, base shape, sharp edges, cap position and intended display orientation. Include any leaflet or insert: it can obstruct the closing flap even when the product itself fits.

State whether operators will assemble the carton by hand or use a packing line. For a line, share the equipment requirements and loading direction with the converter before the dieline is approved. A closure that works on a desk is not automatically compatible with production equipment.
Compare closure behavior

Closure selection before sampling
ClosureWhen to investigate itWhat must be checked
Tuck endAn accessible opening for relatively simple loading and removalFlap retention, friction, product interference and opening direction
Manual lock bottomA base assembled by interlocking flapsAssembly sequence, complete engagement and stability under the actual load
Pre-glued auto bottomA carton whose base forms as the sleeve is openedGlue joints, full opening, base seating and compatibility with the filling process

These are selection starting points, not load ratings. Ask the supplier to identify the exact closure on the drawing because informal names such as “crash lock” can be used inconsistently. Keep the dieline revision beside the material specification.
Specify board and creases together

Board thickness, stiffness, coating and crease design all affect how a carton folds. Increasing grammage alone may make a flap harder to insert or change the finished fit. Request the board grade and thickness alongside GSM; compare a production-representative sample rather than choosing from a weight number alone.

Pro Carton describes carton manufacture as a sequence including printing, cutting, creasing and folding/gluing. The practical implication for the buyer is that the printed sheet and the assembled box need separate checks. Inspect fold edges for visible damage and verify that decoration near a crease still meets the agreed appearance reference. See the board specification guide for the difference between material descriptions.
Check the product and insert as one assembly

A carton may close when empty and bow when loaded. If the insert lifts the bottle, the cap can press on the lid; if the base is narrow, the load may concentrate at an unsupported point. Review the complete loaded carton upright and in the orientations expected during packing. Do not use the top flap to force an oversized product into place.

For a pump bottle, check actuator and cap clearance separately. Product support should come from a deliberately designed base or insert, not accidental pressure on a pump. The carton also needs external transport protection when the distribution route requires it.
Run a repeatable sample comparison

• Assemble several samples using the proposed packing instructions; record any ambiguous fold or missed lock.
  • Load the actual filled product, insert and leaflet, then close without distorting the panels.
  • Inspect base engagement and glue areas, and agree a load-handling evaluation with the supplier.
  • Open and remove the product as a customer would; check tearing, snagging and access.
  • Review a printed sample for cracking, scuffing and artwork hidden by flaps.

If comparing assembly effort, use the same packing task and document the conditions. Do not assume an auto bottom saves a particular number of seconds without observing the actual operation. A faster assembly can still be unsuitable if product positioning becomes unreliable.
Freeze the closure before final artwork

Changing a bottom or flap after artwork approval can move folds, glue areas and panel boundaries. Confirm the structure first, issue artwork on the approved dieline, and retain a signed or otherwise traceable assembled reference. Record the loading direction in the pack-out instructions so a later team does not reverse it.

This guide addresses folding-carton assembly. For the earlier decision between box families, use rigid box vs folding carton vs corrugated packaging.
Technical reference
Pro Carton: carton production explains the manufacturing stages. Closure suitability and load performance remain project-specific and require sample evaluation; no test result is claimed here.
cta: Send the filled product dimensions and weight, intended loading direction, packing method and quantity. MTT can review closure options and the samples needed before artwork is finalized.

title: Corrugated Mailer or Shipping Carton: What to Specify
seoTitle: Corrugated Mailer & Shipping Carton Specs | MTT Packaging
summary: Build a corrugated box specification for comparable quotes: structure, board, inserts, closure, print, packing and sample acceptance before production.
intro: Specify a corrugated mailer or shipping carton as a complete packed system: contents, internal fit, box style, board construction, insert, sealing method and delivery route. Give each supplier the same drawing revision and acceptance criteria. Approve a filled sample before freezing the specification, and agree which transport checks it needs. A flute letter, FEFCO style code or attractive printed sample cannot establish shipping performance on its own.
imageAlt: Corrugated skincare mailer design reference with separated product compartments
faq: What if I do not know the board grade for my shipping box?

Send the filled product weight, packing arrangement, route and handling requirements. Ask the supplier to propose a board construction and verification plan, identifying assumptions. Approve the resulting sample and specification before treating the proposed grade as fixed.
Can a plain white sample approve a printed corrugated mailer?

It can approve the structural features it accurately represents, such as fit and assembly. Keep color, print registration, finish behavior and any material differences open until a representative finished sample has been reviewed. State the scope of each approval in writing.
Does a FEFCO code or an ECT value replace a transport test?

No. A FEFCO code identifies a design; ECT describes board edge-crush performance under a specified method. Neither evaluates the complete filled pack through its intended route. Agree with the customer and testing provider what verification that configuration needs.
sections: Decide what the box must do

Start the brief with one sentence: what is packed, how many units it contains, and which part of the journey this box must survive. A skincare subscription mailer going directly to a consumer has a different job from a master carton carrying retail cartons to a distributor. If the distributor repacks the goods, identify the protection that remains for the next journey.

Then state the appearance requirement. Is a scuffed outer surface acceptable if the contents arrive intact, or must the shipping box itself remain presentable as a gift? The second brief may need a different print finish, protective outer layer or acceptance limit. Decide this before comparing prices.

Structure candidates and the decision that needs a sample
CandidateUseful starting pointCheck before choosing
Roll-end mailerOne set with a controlled opening sequenceSide-wall assembly, locking-tab engagement, sealing and packed outer size
Slotted shipping cartonGrouped units or an outer transport layerFlap closure, tape application, dividers and how the contents carry load
Sleeve and traySliding presentation within a defined shipping systemTray restraint, exposed ends and whether an additional outer is needed

The FEFCO code gives corrugated designs shared identifiers. Use the applicable code alongside an approved drawing showing any modifications. It communicates construction; it does not approve your product, board or route.
Use one specification sheet for every supplier

Copy the fields below into the request for quotation. Mark an undecided field as supplier proposal required, with the assumption to be priced. A blank field invites suppliers to quote different solutions without making the difference visible.

RFQ specification sheet: what to state and what to receive back
FieldBuyer inputSupplier confirmation
ContentsSKU, product photos, filled mass, dimensions, quantity per pack and fragile featuresProduct versions used for the proposal and any missing samples
Structure and fitStyle reference, packing orientation and required usable spaceDrawing revision, dimension convention, units and agreed tolerances
BoardKnown construction or performance needs; request a proposal if unknownWall construction, flute, liner/medium description, caliper and agreed test requirements
Insert and closureItem separation, opening needs, tamper evidence or returns requirementInsert drawing/material, tape or adhesive-strip specification and sealing sequence
Print and finishArtwork version, printed faces, color references and label areaPrint process, substrate, finish, proof method and visual acceptance reference
DistributionParcel or pallet stages, stacking/storage conditions and destinationProposed verification scope and assumptions requiring customer or lab confirmation
Supply formatDelivery quantity, receiving constraints and manual or machine assemblyFlat or assembled supply, bundle/carton counts, packing dimensions and identification
Approval and changesWho approves structure, appearance and transport performanceSample IDs, open issues, revision record and change-notification agreement

Record usable internal dimensions separately from the measured outside of the packed box. Folded walls, inserts and closures can occupy space inside the nominal footprint. Use the internal and external dimension guide for measurement procedure; do not assume a universal clearance or derive the dieline from product size alone.
Translate the board description into something verifiable

“Brown B-flute” leaves several purchasing decisions open. Ask for the proposed board combination and the performance measurements relevant to the job. Where a value is specified, identify its units, test method, sample conditioning and acceptance basis. Supplier grade names need a written definition before they can be compared across quotes.

FEFCO lists separate tests for board edgewise crush, bursting strength and water absorptiveness, as well as compression resistance of packaging. These describe different properties. A board test result should not be presented as proof that a filled box will survive the whole delivery route.

Engineering judgment: first identify the likely failure. A side wall folding under stacking load calls for a review of board, box geometry and load support. A loose glass jar needs restraint and protection; merely upgrading the outer board may leave the jar moving. A damaged printed face calls for a surface and handling review. Do not order “stronger board” until the failure mechanism is understood.

For the specific tradeoff between profiles, see E-flute versus B-flute corrugated boxes. Keep that choice attached to the approved construction rather than treating a flute letter as a quality grade.
Specify the insert and shipping seal together

An insert should support the product where it can accept load, separate vulnerable parts and allow removal. Review the cap, pump, projecting corners and decorative surfaces, not just the widest product outline. A larger cavity may ease packing but permit movement; a tighter cavity may grip a label or load a fragile neck. Confirm the intended contact locations with the actual filled product.

Illustrative example: a mailer contains a tall pump bottle and a squat glass jar. The bottle base is located, but its upper body can swing toward the jar when the pack is turned. Before adding board thickness, we would review upper restraint, separation and the available clearance around the pump. A separate support or revised cavity may be a candidate; its effectiveness still requires evaluation. This is a design scenario, not a reported MTT project or test.

Write down the dispatch closure, including tape type and width or adhesive-strip arrangement, application location and operator sequence. A tuck lock that holds on the packing bench still needs assessment as part of the sealed shipping system. If a return strip or tear strip is requested, check opening and resealing separately. Keep the shipping-label area clear of the intended opening feature. The insert selection guide covers material and support options.
Approve structure, appearance and transport separately

A white structural sample can answer fit and assembly questions. It cannot establish production color, finish durability or all the behavior of a different final board. Record which materials and processes the sample represents. If a temporary insert, dummy product or substitute tape is used, list the questions still open.

  1. Fit and packing: assemble the proposed box, pack every component, close it and remove the contents. Record snagging, distortion, unseated locks and product contact.
  2. Appearance: review a representative printed/finished sample against the artwork and agreed visual limits. Include creases, exposed edges, panel alignment and the label position.
  3. Transport: agree the route, procedure and acceptance criteria with the customer and testing provider. Evaluate the representative product, insert, box and closure together.
  4. Release: record the accepted drawing, board, artwork, sample IDs and remaining conditions. Identify the person responsible for closing each condition before production.

ISTA distinguishes screening tests from general simulation tests. Its selection guidance calls for understanding the distribution environment, using representative samples and setting product-damage and package-degradation criteria before testing. Ask the testing provider to confirm the applicable current procedure and edition.

Define pass/fail in terms the buyer can inspect: for example, no leakage or breakage, acceptable product function, and an agreed limit for visible damage to the presentation surface. These are categories to agree, not universal allowances. A transport report must identify the tested configuration; it is not evidence of food-contact suitability, barrier performance or a supplier-wide certification. Requirements in those areas need their own applicable evidence.
Compare quotes by scope, not just box price

Require a base quotation against the same specification, with alternatives listed separately. Otherwise, a quote for a plain flat box can appear cheaper than one that includes printed interiors, assembled inserts and protective export packing. The unit prices describe different purchases.

Resolve these differences before awarding the order
Comparison itemQuestion for each supplier
Technical departuresWhich board, drawing, finish or packing detail differs from the requested revision?
Included componentsAre inserts, tape/strips, labels, assembly and export packing included or separate?
One-time chargesWhat is charged for samples, cutting tools, print setup and testing, and what is reusable?
Delivered basisAre quantity, currency, trade term, named delivery point and freight/tax inclusions the same?
ScheduleWhen does the quoted lead time start, which approvals does it depend on, and is transit included?
Approval evidenceWhich sample and test commitments are included, and what remains to be confirmed?

Compare packed outer dimensions as well as supply volume. FedEx Canada explains that its dimensional-weight charges can exceed actual-weight charges. Check the current rules for the actual carrier, service and market; do not use a single divisor for every shipment. A smaller parcel is worth evaluating only if the revised protection and packing process remain acceptable.

Do a packing trial before assigning a labor saving to a structure. A more elaborate mailer may replace a separate component, but it may also add folding steps. Keep these as measured or quoted project inputs, not assumed savings.
Carry the approved revision into production and reorders

Attach the approved specification to the purchase order and packing instructions. Keep a reference sample that identifies its revision and approval purpose. Incoming checks can then compare the supplied board description, dimensions, print, insert count and closure against the same record used by procurement.

Reopen the relevant approval when the filled product weight, product shape, quantity per box, board combination, insert, closure, finish or distribution route changes. Record the proposed change and ask the responsible engineer or test provider which checks must be repeated. A supplier should not silently substitute a similar-looking board under the old sample approval.

As a China Packaging Development & Manufacturing Partner, MTT can help turn the brief into structural proposals, samples and production-coordination requirements. The useful next step is a reviewable packed specification, with unconfirmed assumptions visible.
cta: Send product photos, filled weights and dimensions, quantity per box, order quantity and the delivery route, plus any existing drawing or failed pack. MTT can review the corrugated specification, identify missing decisions and propose a sampling scope.

title: Paper Bag Dimensions: Size, Handles and Sample Checks
seoTitle: Paper Bag Dimensions: Size in mm & Inches | MTT
summary: Measure paper bag width, gusset and height, convert mm to inches, and check usable space, handles and loaded samples before ordering custom bags.
intro: Size a custom paper bag around the finished contents in their carrying orientation, including tissue and accessories. Specify width, side gusset and height with a drawing. Choose handles and reinforcement around the loaded weight and intended use, then evaluate an assembled, loaded sample. Paper weight and a premium handle finish do not establish a safe carrying capacity by themselves.
imageAlt: Paper shopping bag design reference showing handles and a reinforced opening
sections: Measure the finished pack, not the product cavity

Use the external dimensions of the assembled box or the complete set that will enter the bag. Show its insertion orientation. For multiple items, document the arrangement rather than adding individual dimensions without accounting for their positions. Tissue, ribbons and protruding lids can change the clearance required.

Label width, gusset and height on the drawing. Ask whether the quoted dimensions are finished measurements and how they are checked. Leave handling clearance based on a physical trial; there is no single allowance that suits every stiff box, paper grade or presentation style. For coordinated fragrance sets, see box and bag planning.
Paper bag size chart: label each measurement

Use width × gusset × height in the purchase brief, with each axis labelled on the drawing. A size written as three numbers is easy to misread when another supplier uses a different order. Record the measurement basis as well as the units.

Paper bag dimensions to confirm with the supplier
DimensionWhat to identifyFit check
WidthThe front-face width, with reference edges marked.Can the packed box pass through the opening without forcing it?
GussetThe side depth when the bag is opened for use.Does the complete pack sit on the base without bowing the sides?
HeightThe bag body from the base to the top edge; record handles separately.Do contents, tissue and closures leave the required space below the grip?
Handle clearanceThe usable space between the top edge and the grip.Can a person carry the loaded sample comfortably?

This is a measurement chart, not a stock-size catalogue. Names such as small, medium or large do not specify a fit. Ask for the actual dimensions and check usable space with the contents installed; top folds, reinforcement and handle attachments can interfere with insertion.
Convert paper bag dimensions between mm and inches

Inches = millimetres ÷ 25.4. Millimetres = inches × 25.4. NIST defines one inch as exactly 25.4 mm.[1] Convert width, gusset and height separately, keeping the same order.

Unit conversion only — not recommended bag sizes
MillimetresInches (rounded to two decimals)
100 mm3.94 in
200 mm7.87 in
250 mm9.84 in
300 mm11.81 in

Keep one agreed unit as the controlling dimension on the approved drawing. Mark the converted figures as reference values: rounding a conversion is not permission to change the size or its tolerance. Conversion also does not turn an external measurement into usable internal space. Use the internal and external dimension guide when measuring the box that goes inside the bag.
Select handles by use and attachment

Handle choices to evaluate on a loaded sample
Handle optionBuyer considerationCheck at sampling
RibbonVisual coordination and feel in the handAttachment, slipping, edge discomfort and available hand clearance
CordProfile, grip and attachment detailKnot or fastening retention, hole areas and reinforcement
Flat paper handlePaper-based appearance and a different attachment areaBonded area, peeling and carrying comfort under the intended load
Die-cut openingNo separate handle componentOpening shape, reinforcement and tearing around the grip

These options do not have fixed load capacities. The paper, reinforcement, attachment geometry, adhesive and contents all matter. Ask for the complete construction to be documented, including details hidden inside the folded top.
Review the base and top reinforcement

A flat-bottomed gift box and several loose bottles load a bag differently. Inspect how the contents sit on the base and whether a corner creates a local pressure point. Check the base fold, bonded areas and any base insert as a system. Reinforcing only the handles does not resolve a weak base.

Review the folded top and handle attachment from inside the bag as well as outside. A neat exterior can hide inconsistent bonding or an interfering handle knot. If a removable base board is proposed, include it in packing instructions and in every loaded evaluation.
Approve appearance alongside carrying behavior

A smooth bag paper can reproduce color and foil differently from a textured box wrap. Approve the set together using agreed physical references. Check where the folded edges, gussets and handle holes interrupt the artwork; keep essential information away from uncertain trim and fold boundaries.

Read matching foil across boxes and bags for coordinated finish approval. Scuffing and moisture exposure should be discussed for the expected use. Do not call a paper bag waterproof or assign an environmental claim simply because of its appearance or paper content.
Write a loaded-sample evaluation brief

• List the complete contents and combined weight, including the presentation box and accessories.
  • Insert and remove the set without forcing the opening or catching decoration.
  • Check hand clearance and comfort with the intended handle length.
  • Agree carrying, lifting and hold conditions with the supplier, then document the observations.
  • Inspect the handle area, top fold, seams and base for changes after the agreed evaluation.
  • Record the exact paper, handles, reinforcement and adhesive construction of the approved sample.

Set acceptance conditions before evaluating samples. A single successful lift is only an observation under that condition, not a certified load rating. If the contents or construction change, review whether another sample evaluation is needed.
Specify packing and the next purchasing step

Paper bags can arrive flattened, with handles arranged in different ways. Confirm the packing method, quantity per shipping carton and protection against surface marking. Check whether the receiving team can store the bags and prepare them without damaging handles or creases.

A carrying bag does not replace a parcel shipping system. Use the corrugated transport-pack guide when the contents will be sent by courier. For a reorder, preserve the approved construction and sample reference instead of ordering only by size and color. This article provides a project checklist; it does not claim an MTT load test or a universal carrying limit.
Source and measurement boundaries

[1] NIST: SI Units – Length, checked 28 October 2026, supports the inch-to-millimetre conversion. The table values are calculated from that definition.

The measurement chart is a specification checklist, not a published MTT customer case, production drawing or load-test result. Confirm the bag construction, usable space and carrying performance on the agreed sample.
cta: Send the finished contents, carrying orientation, total loaded weight, preferred handle, quantity and artwork. MTT can review bag dimensions, reinforcement choices and a loaded-sample evaluation brief.

title: Packaging Reorders: Control Specifications and Version Changes
summary: Prepare a packaging reorder with approved samples, material versions and change records. Separate repeat production from changes that need renewed evaluation.
intro: A packaging reorder should reference an approved specification and sample, not just an old purchase order or photograph. Confirm that the product, material, artwork, insert, packing method and delivery route are unchanged. Record every proposed substitution or revision before production. When a change affects fit, appearance or transport performance, agree the sample or test evidence needed to approve the revised configuration.
imageAlt: Rigid presentation box reference for checking a reorder against an approved configuration
sections: Build a single approved specification record

A buyer may retain the final artwork while the packing team uses an older insert drawing. A reorder can then reproduce different versions of the same set. Assign a revision to the complete packaging configuration, and reference the component revisions beneath it. The purchase order should identify that record.

Keep a physical sample where practical and record its approval date, relevant signatures or written approval, and any accepted exceptions. Photographs help identify the configuration but cannot fully describe color, surface feel, opening resistance or material construction. Start with the sample approval checklist if the original approval is incomplete.
Separate unchanged repeats from revisions

Reorder change review
ChangePossible consequenceEvidence to review
Bottle, cap or accessory dimensionsFit, support or removal may changeActual product and loaded fit sample
Board, wrap, adhesive or insert materialAppearance, assembly or protection may differUpdated specification and representative sample
Artwork or decorationColor, registration or legibility may changeArtwork proof and affected finish reference
Pack-out quantity or shipping routeThe transport system may face different loadsUpdated packing plan and test review
No proposed changeStored references and current production still need alignmentWritten specification confirmation and agreed production checks

This table is a review trigger, not an automatic instruction to repeat every test. Decide the necessary evidence from the consequence of the change. Record who accepts that decision.
Do not approve a substitution by description alone

“Equivalent paper” is incomplete if the original specification includes texture, thickness or printing behavior. Ask what is changing and why. Review the characteristics that matter for this pack, including any documented claim that depends on material sourcing. A matching color name does not show that foil or adhesive will behave in the same way.

Separate a proposed substitute from the approved baseline. Record whether it is accepted for one order or becomes the new standard. If acceptance is conditional, state the unresolved checks so the next reorder does not treat a temporary exception as permanent approval.
Keep component quantities and versions aligned

For sets, list box, insert, sleeve, bag and printed accessories individually. Show the quantity and artwork version of each. One shared outer box can support several inserts, but a picking mistake may create a set that looks correct and fits poorly. Use an understandable component identifier in the packing instructions.

The shared-box guide covers the initial decision to standardize a shell. On reorder, check whether the SKU combinations and actual products are still the same. Do not silently use an earlier insert because it remains in stock.
Revisit transport evidence when the system changes

ISTA guidance on retesting identifies changes to the product, packaging and distribution system as reasons to review retesting. Keep the evaluated configuration identifiable so a report is not assumed to cover an altered pack.

Discuss the effect of the change with the testing provider or responsible customer team. A different insert, product weight or pack-out can matter even when the outer box dimensions are unchanged. Record the decision and its basis; do not describe a changed configuration as tested unless the supporting evidence applies to it.
Use a pre-production reorder checklist

• Confirm the complete configuration and component revision numbers.
  • Confirm current product samples or written confirmation that the product is unchanged.
  • List changes and substitutions explicitly, including a written “none” when appropriate.
  • Agree the reference sample, appearance criteria and inspection scope.
  • Confirm quantities by version, packing instructions and shipping-carton markings.
  • Confirm stock treatment and delivery arrangements separately from new production.

For inventory already produced, read storage and scheduled delivery. Releasing approved stock is a different decision from manufacturing a new batch. For new production, reconfirm timing and price from the current specification rather than assuming the previous order terms still apply.
Resolve discrepancies before release

If the sample, drawing and order disagree, stop treating any one of them as automatically authoritative. Identify the discrepancy, obtain a clear written decision and update the affected references. Archive the previous revision so it remains traceable but cannot be mistaken for the current production instruction.

This is a purchasing control framework, not a claim about a completed customer reorder. It helps a buyer decide what must be reconfirmed and what evidence belongs with the next order.
cta: Send the previous approved specification, sample reference, current product details and a list of proposed changes. MTT can review which components need reconfirmation before a reorder specification is released.
